title: Pray for the government (Avot 3:2)
hook: Chanina: pray for the welfare of the government, for without order people would swallow each other
tomorrow: two friends, one table, one line between them. who else shows up?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akavia's three questions: whence, whither, before whom. They kept a title small enough to turn down. Today, the next sage in the chapter, and a strange word he picks.

Take the admins out of a group chat for a week and watch. The loudest voices take over, the quiet ones go silent, and somebody posts the same meme over and over. Yesterday's question was why pray for the people in charge, even ones you argue with. Rabbi Chanina, the deputy of the priests, gives his reason in Avot: pray for the welfare of the government, because without the fear of it, people would swallow each other alive. Swallow. Not fight, not cheat. Swallow. Why that word?
screen: `NO ADMINS FOR A WEEK.` → `PRAY FOR THE GOVERNMENT'S WELFARE.` → `OR PEOPLE WOULD SWALLOW EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: The Talmud solves the puzzle with a line from the prophet Habakkuk. He complains that people are made "as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them." In the sea, the Talmud says, the bigger fish swallows the smaller. Among people, without order, the bigger would swallow the smaller too. So the prayer isn't flattery of whoever rules. It's for the small fish. Order protects the weakest first. Second, look at what the prayer asks for: shlomah shel malchut, the government's welfare, its peace. Not its victories, not a ruler's fame. An older voice said it to exiles. Jeremiah writes to the captives carried off to Babylon: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." A city that wasn't even theirs. Third, praying for isn't the same as agreeing with. Some synagogues say a prayer for the country and its leaders on Shabbat, and the people saying it still argue about every decision. The wish is for steady order, the kind that keeps the strong from swallowing the weak. Fourth, the ordinary version: a red light at an empty intersection, a referee, a fire code. Small pieces of the same idea.
screen: `FISH WITH NO RULER.` · `THE PRAYER IS FOR THE SMALL FISH.` · `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.` · `PRAYING FOR ISN'T AGREEING WITH.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR ORDER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person with authority over part of your life: a manager, a principal, a mayor, a coach. Wish them well at the job itself, steady judgment, a calm head on a hard day, whatever you think of their choices. If you pray, you can name them before God, the way some congregations name their leaders each Shabbat.
Pray for the government: Rabbi Chanina's saying, a prayer for order itself, because order is what keeps the small fish safe.
Your line: pray for order. The peace of the city is your peace too. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: your apartment's tenant board is slow and annoying, and a neighbor says let's just ignore its rules. what does Rabbi Chanina's saying point to?
options: push to fix it, but keep the order that guards the weakest.
ignore it; the saying only covers kings and empires.
obey in silence; any questioning is the real danger.
fork.reveal: the saying protects the small fish. it asks for the welfare of the order, which leaves room to argue about how it's run.

chat.says: principal says rehearsals end at 6 sharp now. eleven days out!! why do schools need SO many rules?
options: Without order the big fish swallow the small. Argue the 6 p.m. part, but want the rules.
Rules are always right; Avot says pray for leaders, so never argue with them.
Avot means pray only for good leaders; a bad rule doesn't deserve it.
chat.meaning: Rabbi Chanina prays for order because it protects the weakest. Wanting order and arguing about one rule can go together.
